studies.title: Prayer Without Attention
studies.meaning: The surah begins by asking about a person who denies the reckoning and then answers with behaviour rather than belief. He shoves the orphan and does not urge that the poor be fed. The second failure is not even a refusal to give; it is a failure to encourage giving. Then the address turns to people who do pray, and the woe is transferred to them, which is the surah's shock.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan by the tradition this collection follows, though several classical authorities read the second half as Medinan because of what it says about those who pray. The reports name particular Meccans as the occasion of the opening, and they do not agree on which. The orphan is the recurring figure. Mecca had many, and their property was easy to take.

keyTerms.note: A verb of physical shoving rather than of refusing. The picture is a hand on a child, which makes the failure visible and public rather than a matter of what someone declined to do.
A verb of pushing someone toward an action with words. What is named is not withholding but silence: the man is faulted for not encouraging other people to feed the poor.
From a verb for forgetting through inattention rather than through a lapse of memory. The preposition attached to it points at the prayer itself, so the absence is from what is being done.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An orphan's inheritance sat with whoever took him in, and there was no court to review the arrangement. A child with property and no father was a temptation, and Meccan society knew it. The physical detail in this surah is a shove. It describes what happened when such a child asked for something and the man holding his money was tired of him.
studies.didYouKnow: The word of woe in this surah is not aimed at the person who denies the reckoning. It is aimed at people who pray. That redirection, in the fourth of seven very short lines, is one of the sharpest turns in the Quran, and the surah then finishes by naming the smallest kind of help as what such people withhold.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The surah makes belief testable by conduct toward people who cannot complain. Denying the reckoning is not described as an opinion. It is described as a hand pushing a child. Then the same test is applied to worshippers. That removes prayer as a defence and makes it evidence to be looked at rather than a credential. The two halves together say that ritual and the treatment of the weak are one question.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same two instructions in the positive, addressed to someone who was once an orphan himself.
Pairs the same two failures, using the identical verb about urging others to feed.
States what prayer is supposed to do, which is what the heedless prayer in this surah is not doing.

studies.applyIt: Say one prayer this week where you know what you said. Not a longer prayer, the same length, but with your attention actually on the words for its duration. Most people find they cannot manage a whole one at first. The surah's complaint is about absence during the act, so the test is simply whether you were there.
studies.explainEasier: God asks who really turns his back on the faith. It is the man who pushes an orphan away, and does not tell people to feed the poor. Then God warns those who pray but pay no attention to their prayer.

studies.title: Withholding The Small Kindness
studies.meaning: Two relative clauses finish the description, and both concern appearance and access. The first names people who act in order to be seen acting, using a verb form that requires an audience to exist at all. The second names what they refuse, and the commentators divide openly over the word: the small everyday things neighbours lend each other, or the formal alms, or assistance of any kind. Every reading keeps the withheld thing minor. The chapter ends not on a great crime but on a borrowed bucket.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan according to most of the classical sources, with some placing part of the chapter in Medina; the disagreement is recorded rather than settled. Either setting puts the audience at close quarters in a settlement where households borrowed from each other daily and a refusal was noticed the same hour. Commentators read the closing pair of lines as the surah's turn from public worship to private neighbourliness.

keyTerms.note: A reciprocal form built from the verb to see, meaning to act so as to be observed doing it. The form implies onlookers, so the fault it names cannot occur when a person is alone.

Occurring only here in the Quran, and the commentators disagree about it more openly than about almost any word in the short chapters. Readings run from a neighbour's cooking pot to the obligatory alms.
A verb of preventing access rather than of failing to give. It describes an active refusal of something already asked for, which is why the small size of the thing refused matters so much.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Households ran on constant small lending. A cooking pot, a bucket for the well, a hand mill, a measure of salt, a needle. Nobody owned everything and the borrowing went in every direction, which meant the system worked only because refusing was close to unthinkable. A man who said no to a bucket was announcing that he had stepped outside the arrangement keeping everyone around him fed.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for what is withheld occurs once in the entire Quran, and the classical commentators set out at least three different meanings for it without choosing. Al-Tabari lists the readings side by side. A chapter of seven lines therefore ends on the one word in it whose sense the tradition has never settled.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The final measure is the smallest possible act. Having begun with a man who denies the reckoning and passed through people who pray without attention, the chapter tests them on a household utensil, and the scale of evidence runs opposite to the scale of importance. A person can manage a large donation in front of witnesses. What he does with a neighbour's request at an inconvenient hour is much harder to arrange.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for standing in prayer to be seen by people, with reluctance underneath it.
Describes charity cancelled by display, spending wealth to be seen by people rather than for God.
Pairs the same two failures, the orphan and the feeding of the poor, as evidence about a whole society.

studies.applyIt: Say yes to the next small thing somebody asks you for, even if it is slightly inconvenient and even if you suspect they could manage without it. A tool, a lift, ten minutes. Do it once and pay attention to how quickly the reasons for saying no assemble themselves. That speed is what the chapter is pointing at.
